title: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (2 of 7)
hook: a monk in New York tells office workers the secret of work
tomorrow: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (3 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma yoga. Whatever you do, eat or give, done as an offering, doesn't bind.

New York. A Hindu monk stands at the front of a room, and his listeners aren't monks. They have jobs to get back to. He's not telling them to leave those jobs. He's telling them how to do them. A monk, of all people, giving lessons on how to work. He is Swami Vivekananda, a disciple of Sri Ramakrishna, and the talks were written down and became a small book, Karma-Yoga. Today, its core.
screen: `A MONK IN NEW YORK.` → `NOT TALKING TO MONKS.` → `HOW TO DO YOUR JOB.`

segments.voice: Vivekananda starts with character. Every action, he says, leaves an impression on the mind, a samskara, like a groove. Do a thing often enough and the groove deepens, until the sum of your grooves is your character. So a person is made not by one great deed but by thousands of small ones. Ordinary work is building you, whether you notice or not. Then comes what he calls the secret of work: work, but don't be attached. Be like a master, not a slave. The slave works for the wage, the praise, the result, and is miserable when they don't come. The master works because the work is worth doing, and is free either way. The misery, he says plainly, comes from attachment, not from the work. You can pour yourself into a job and still not be owned by how it turns out. That's the Gita's line, the right to the action, never to the fruit, made to sound like advice for Monday morning. He's honest that it's hard. Non-attachment isn't coldness; it's not caring less. One way to see it: a mother up all night with a sick child isn't detached from the child. She just isn't waiting to be thanked. Then a twist. Doing good in the world, he says, helps us more than it helps the world: it's our own training. In his view, that's why to offer the work: not because the world needs anyone's help so badly, but because giving it is how a person is made free.
screen: `EVERY ACT LEAVES A GROOVE.` · `THE SECRET OF WORK.` · `A MASTER, NOT A SLAVE.` · `NOT COLDNESS: NOT OWNED BY THE RESULT.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Think of a piece of work you're worried about, how it'll land, who'll notice, and feel where that worry sits in your body. Gently separate the two: the work, which you can do well, and the result, which isn't yours to hold. Breathe in and take up the work; breathe out and set down the result, master, not slave.
Asakta, unattached. Vivekananda's secret of work: work fully, but be a master, not a slave, unattached to the result.
Your line: offer the work. Every act you do leaves a groove. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Swami Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga is read in Vedanta societies and beyond; the Ramakrishna Mission he founded treats service to others as a form of worship.

fork.setup: you've worked hard on something and nobody thanked you. what would Vivekananda say?
options: you worked as a master; the result was never yours to hold.
fork.reveal: work like a master, not a slave. the misery comes from attachment to the result, not from the work.

original.note: Sanskrit: asakta, unattached; Gita 3.19 asks for work done asakta, without attachment.

trapdoor: what you thought: non-attachment means not caring.
what it means: work with everything you have, and don't let the result own you.
what a scholar hears: Vivekananda's chapters include 'the secret of work' and 'we help ourselves, not the world'; the samskara idea draws on Yoga philosophy.
guess: unattached: working fully without clinging to results
uninterested: not caring how the work turns out
unmoving: refusing to act so nothing can bind you
